Introduction
Although the requisite growing pains have existed along the way, Yukon has progres
sed almost steadily since June 13, 1898, when it was officially designated as a distinct
jurisdiction of Canada under the terms of the Yukon Act.
The Act also provided for a Territorial Government, consisting of a Commissioner and
an appointed Council.
The first wholly-elected Council took office in 1909, and consisted of eleven Members.
But this number has fluctuated over the years in accordance with population figures:
today's Legislative Assembly is comprised of sixteen Members, representing each of
Yukon's electoral districts.
Coupled with these continual advances, Yukon held its first election along party lines in
the fall of November, 1978, with the Progressive Conservatives securing the majority of
seats.

Up to and including that time, the actions of the governing Executive Committee were
subject to the consent of the Commissioner, who was and still is, the federal govern
ment's senior public servant in Yukon.
However, in October, 1979, the terms of reference for the Commissioner were altered
substantially by the federal Progressive Conservative government.
As a result of this, the Executive Committee was allowed to change its name to the
Executive Council, or Cabinet, and authorized to make decisions on its own.
While the government of Yukon has always publicized its decisions, regulations,
notices and other official matters, this information was relayed only through local
newspapers and was not available for reference purposes in a formal manner.
Newspapers will still be utilized when the need arises, but the monthly compilation of
government matters in this Gazette is clearly another step in the evolution of responsi
ble government in Yukon.
